## Task statement

**Invariant.** Every outbound fetch connects only to the public address it validated, re-checks per hop, is capped

**Oracle.** fake resolver + mock transport record the actual destination

**Violation cases seeded.** redirect to non-public; rebinding resolver; off-list host; oversize body

Source: `EVALS-PLAN.md` Layer 0.

## Construction

Every task is a directory `evals/cases/P4/<case>/` holding a `case.yaml` (the task record: `id`, `property`, `origin`, `grader`, `expect`, `description`, `canary`), a `vuln/` tree with exactly one planted violation, and a `clean/` twin — the same code with the violation fixed through the toolkit primitive. The grader scores both: the violation must be detected in `vuln/` (recall) and not in `clean/` (precision), so the clean twin is the baseline scored alongside every task.

Origins, in the priority order of EVALS-PLAN.md Layer 2:

- **historical-miss** (3): a real miss from this program, encoded permanently.
- **derived** (2): a violation case from the Layer 0 row, in a code shape the historical cases do not already cover.

| task | origin | grader | description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `P4-content-derived-url-01` | historical-miss | `egress` | study-hub sync_piazza: hrefs scraped out of a fetched resources page were downloaded as-is, so a link in the page's content chose the destination. vuln follows every href with a raw client; clean host-checks each href against the allow-list and downloads through safe_fetch. |
| `P4-cron-sibling-raw-client-01` | historical-miss | `egress` | smart-dispatch data_ingestion: ingest_recent was moved to safe_fetch while its cron sibling ingest_ercot_history kept a raw client with follow_redirects on, and the sibling is the one the nightly job calls. vuln keeps both functions in one module with the entry point routed to the raw one; clean routes both through the shared _fetch helper over safe_fetch with the ERCOT allow-list. |
| `P4-dns-rebinding-01` | derived | `egress` | Validate-then-connect-by-name: the resolver is consulted for the check and again by the client for the connection, so an answer that changes between the two lookups reaches a non-public address. clean connects to the exact address it validated (safe_fetch pins the IP and sends the real Host/SNI). |
| `P4-off-list-uncapped-01` | derived | `egress` | A client class for one known service that accepts any URL it is handed and reads the whole body: no allow-list, no byte cap. clean passes the service's allow_hosts and a max_bytes to safe_fetch, so an off-list URL and an oversize body are both refused. |
| `P4-redirect-to-loopback-01` | historical-miss | `egress` | The classic SSRF guard: the start URL's host is resolved and checked, then a raw client follows redirects by name, so a 302 to a loopback or private address is connected to with the check already passed. clean uses safe_fetch, which re-validates every hop and never auto-follows. |

## Metrics and current numbers

- **recall** = tasks whose `vuln/` the grader detected ÷ tasks, Wilson 95% CI.
- **precision** = tasks whose `clean/` the grader did not flag ÷ tasks, Wilson 95% CI.
- with `--trials K > 1`: **pass@k** (any of k) and **pass^k** (all of k) over tasks.

## Known limitations

From the grader docstrings (what each oracle can and cannot decide):

### `egress`

> P4 egress grader (plugin): where did the fetcher actually connect?
>
>     egress   expect: {target: "mod:fn", allowed_hosts: [...], max_bytes: N,
>                       scenarios: [redirect_private, redirect_loopback, rebinding,
>                                   off_list, derived_links, oversize]}
>
> The target is `fn(url, *, resolver, transport)`. The grader injects a
> getaddrinfo-compatible resolver backed by a table (public, private, loopback and
> a flapping answer) and an `httpx.MockTransport` that records every request and
> serves scripted responses (redirects, link pages, oversize bodies). Nothing
> touches the network.
>
> Detected = in any scenario the recorded connection sequence reaches a non-public
> address, a host outside `allowed_hosts`, or the function hands back more than
> `max_bytes`. A hostname in a recorded request is resolved *again* at
> "connect time" through the same resolver, which is what a real client would do:
> a fetcher that validates the name and then connects by name is caught by the
> flapping answer (DNS rebinding); one that connects to the address it validated
> (`secprim.safe_fetch`) sends IP literals and is not.
>
> Any library can be the vuln as long as it honours the injected transport (httpx
> does); a `requests`-based fetcher cannot be driven offline and is out of scope.

## Contamination policy

- **Canary.** Every `case.yaml`, every registry entry and `tasks.jsonl` carry the string in `evals/registry/CANARY.txt` (BIG-bench convention): a model that can reproduce it has seen this corpus in training, and its scores on it do not measure the property.
- **Split.** This eval is `split: build`. Build-split cases are used to tune rules and defenses. The held-out split (`evals/heldout/`, EVALS-PLAN.md Phase 4) is sealed: written after the defenses, never used for tuning, and scored only in reports.
- **No model in the loop.** Every grader is deterministic code; no LLM judges a result, so there is nothing to contaminate on the grading side.
